item.title: PEOPLE I Learning beyond the village
item.description: AT 24, Raijeli Naceva is learning that motherhood does not have to mean putting her own dreams on hold. For the young mother from Nausori Highland in Namataku, Navosa, every short course is another opportunity to learn something new and build a future in the village.
item.content:encoded:
AT 24, Raijeli Naceva is learning that motherhood does not have to mean putting her own dreams on hold.

For the young mother from Nausori Highland in Namataku, Navosa, every short course is another opportunity to learn something new and build a future in the village.

Raijeli, who has maternal links to the area, grew up in a farming family.

Her parents are farmers, and she is the eldest of six children, with her younger siblings still attending school.

Today, she and her husband, who is also from Nausori Highland, are raising their two-year-old daughter while running a small yaqona farm.

“You know life in the village – it’s mainly chores for us women,” Raijeli said.

For her family, yaqona farming is an important source of livelihood, but Raijeli is also looking beyond the farm, using short courses to broaden her skills and understanding.

She attended Ratu Nalewavada Public School in Nausori Highlands before continuing at Nadi Sangam College from Form 3 to Form 6.

She completed Form 7 at Ratu Navula College before pursuing a Certificate III in Age Care and Community Care.

The course changed how she viewed caring for elderly family members.

“What I learned in age care has broadened my understanding of how to take care of elderly in the family,” she said.

One lesson that stayed with her was the importance of food.

Raijeli learned that what elderly people eat can have a significant impact on their health, particularly when they continue eating foods they have been advised to avoid by the hospital.

She responded by reducing those foods and introducing healthier alternatives available in the village.

Now, her latest learning experience has opened another possibility.

Raijeli took part in tie-dye training, an experience she enjoyed.

“I liked that I was part of it,” she said.

Her goal is to start a small tie-dye business in the village, where she sees a demand for the products.

For Raijeli, learning is becoming part of everyday life alongside motherhood, farming and village responsibilities.

The tie-dye training was part of the buildup to the Navosa Youth Festival held last week.

item.title: PEOPLE | Turning farm labour into opportunity
item.description: WHEN the crowds began arriving at Vatureba Park for the Navosa Youth Festival, Kinisalote Rakai was already at work. At the entrance to the park, the 43-year-old farmer from Nukuilau Village in Draubuta, Navosa, had set up her makeshift stall with freshly harvested watermelons.
item.content:encoded:
WHEN the crowds began arriving at Vatureba Park for the Navosa Youth Festival, Kinisalote Rakai was already at work.

At the entrance to the park, the 43-year-old farmer from Nukuilau Village in Draubuta, Navosa, had set up her makeshift stall with freshly harvested watermelons.

Some were cut into juicy portions for festival-goers looking for something cool in the hot weather, while whole melons were ready for those wanting to take one home.

The location proved to be a good choice.

As people entered the festival, many stopped at Rakai’s stall to buy the affordable watermelon.

By midday, almost 80 of the more than 100 watermelons, she had brought with her husband, had been sold.

“We have been farming for a while, and watermelon has been one of our longest crops as it grows well in the province,” Rakai said.

For Rakai, selling the family’s produce is another part of the work she shares with her husband.

Their farm has been producing watermelons since 1999.

Over 27 years, they have also grown cabbages, tomatoes, capsicum, long beans, bora beans, French beans, corn, peanuts, watermelons and sweet potatoes.

The couple leases land and uses a tractor to help with the work.

They once had a carrier but sold it to buy the tractor because it would help them more in running the farm.

Getting their produce to the market, however, comes at a cost.

Transporting the watermelons from Nukuilau Village to Vatureba Park costs them $180.

The Rakai couple has seven children. After the death of their eldest child, they now care for their six children with what they earn from farming.

She said their experience had shown them that the weather in Navosa allowed certain vegetables to grow well, giving the family an opportunity to earn from the land.

For Rakai, farming is a partnership, and she wants other women to see the value of being part of that partnership.

“I would like to encourage women, who are at home, to always assist your husband if he farms,” she said.

“We can earn a lot if we help each other out in toiling the land.”

At the festival, each watermelon sold was a small return on years of shared labour.

item.title: PEOPLE | From training to trade | New skill builds business hope
item.description: A TWO-DAY training at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga has changed how Joave Doidoi views earning an income. The young man from Draiba Village in the Namataku district of Navosa plans to turn his newly acquired tie-dye skills into a business at home.
item.content:encoded:
A TWO-DAY training at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga has changed how Joave Doidoi views earning an income.

The young man from Draiba Village in the Namataku district of Navosa plans to turn his newly acquired tie-dye skills into a business at home.

With a bubbly personality and an easy manner, Joave spoke enthusiastically about what he learned during the short course.

He was among participants who later showcased their creations at the recent Navosa Youth Festival, an experience that opened his eyes to the possibilities of his new skills.

“Attending the tie-dye and soap making training session lifted many of the worries I had about earning an income,” Joave said.

“I realised from the training session that it’s easy to earn an income right in the village.”

The training also broadened his understanding of how everyday materials could be transformed into income-generating products.

“This has deepened our knowledge, especially on how to use everyday materials at home to make income-generating products like soap, for instance,” he said.

Joave had previously completed a Level 3 Certificate in Catering and Commercial Cookery. When he heard about the tie-dye course, he seized the opportunity.

“When I heard about the tie-dye course, I quickly jumped at the opportunity because I would acquire new skills from it in just two days,” he said.

Although originally from Draiba Village, Joave currently lives at Natao Settlement. He intends to take his skills back home and put them into practice.

“I can see myself starting my own business in the village,” he said.

“I’m planning to go home and actually make something out of what I’ve learned instead of leaving it aside again.”

For Joave, the next step is turning training into action.

He hopes young people who gain skills can receive further support, particularly financial assistance to help establish their projects.

“I can start my own tie-dye project or help others learn about it,” he said.

The two-day training has given him more than a skill — it has given him a plan: to take knowledge home, create products and build an income from his village doorstep.

item.title: PEOPLE I Skill to wealth
item.description: AT 19, Ivamere Finau Kaitoga has already learned that setbacks do not have to determine the direction of a young person’s life. Growing up in Nausori Highlands, in the district of Namataku, Nadroga/Navosa, Ivamere was raised by her mother after her father died when she was only 11 months old.
item.content:encoded:
AT 19, Ivamere Finau Kaitoga has already learned that setbacks do not have to determine the direction of a young person’s life.

Growing up in Nausori Highlands, in the district of Namataku, Nadroga/Navosa, Ivamere was raised by her mother after her father died when she was only 11 months old.

Her mother became the family’s main support and from a young age, Ivamere learnt to stand beside her.

School was one of the challenges she faced.

After completing Form 5, Ivamere left high school and began searching for a different path to shape her future.

She went on to study Business Administration at Pacific Polytech, a decision that would become an important stepping stone in her journey.

During this time, she lived with her uncle in Ba, however, when her uncle’s home was destroyed by a fire, Ivamere was forced to return to her village.

Back home she joined other young people in yaqona farming, a common livelihood for youths in Nausori Highlands.

Her family also depend on her mother, who operates a small canteen from home, grows vegetables and sells produce at the Nadi market, to help meet the family’s daily expenses.

Ivamere and her siblings help their mother every day.

Then came an opportunity that gave the young woman a new way of looking at what was possible.

Ivamere took part in tie-dye training organised by the Ministry of Youth and Sports at the Nasau Training Centre in Nadroga.

For her, the training was more than learning how to create colourful designs. It opened her eyes to the possibility of turning a skill into an income-generating activity while remaining in the village.

“The training has broadened my knowledge and has allowed me to learn a new skill,” she said.

“It was an eye-opener for me as a young woman living in the village, it has taught me that we can earn an income from these types of skills even while living in the village.”

The experience has given Ivamere something to take home besides the skill itself: A plan.

She wants to continue practising tie-dye, create materials in the village and share what she has learnt with her family.

Her aim is to improve her skills until the craft can become a source of income.

Her experience in business administration may also prove useful as she works towards that goal.

Ivamere hopes to combine what she learnt in her studies with her new tie-dye skills.

For a young woman, who faced the loss of her father as an infant, struggled at school and returned to the village after her family lost their home, the future now looks different.

Ivamere is not simply returning home with a new skill, she is returning with an idea of what that skill could become in the future.

item.title: PEOPLE I Creating happy moments
item.description: FOR Ratu Peni Bainiyasikula Salatubalevu, music has become more than a performance. It has opened doors to places he might otherwise never have seen and given him a role in keeping Fiji’s traditions alive.
item.content:encoded:
FOR Ratu Peni Bainiyasikula Salatubalevu, music has become more than a performance.

It has opened doors to places he might otherwise never have seen and given him a role in keeping Fiji’s traditions alive.

From Wailevu Village in Cakaudrove, Vanua Levu, with maternal links to Suweni Village in Wairiki, Cakaudrove, Ratu Peni is a member of the National Youth Brass Marching Band.

His journey with the band began with training in 2022 before he officially became a member in 2023.

“I’ve learned a lot being part of the National Youth Band, it has allowed me to be part of many important events associated with youth development in the country,” he said.

Among those events was the Navosa Youth Festival at Vatureba Park, Navosa this week.

The opportunities have also taken him around Fiji including Rotuma, allowing him to showcase what he describes as the real representation of Fiji.

His instrument is the baritone, a medium-low brass instrument whose pitch range sits between the higher tenor and lower bass.

But his connection to music extends beyond brass.

Ratu Peni also participates in a traditional meke dance group and sings old traditional songs; activities he believes are important in reviving traditions that are slowly dying out.

He is also part of Dolce Sounds Dulali Group, a Fijian performing arts organisation dedicated to preserving, elevating and teaching indigenous traditional folk singing, choral harmony and cultural meke dances.

One of his most memorable performances was at the Pacific Ministers Youth Meeting held in Fiji last year.

His work also takes him into youth awareness activities, where the message is clear: young people should move away from substance abuse and focus on education and sports.

His journey has not always been uninterrupted.

He began attending classes at the National Youth Council of Fiji in Valelevu in 2020, but returned to his village when COVID-19 struck. He later returned and completed his studies.

He was also involved in the Ministry of Justice’s Constitution Review Commission youth consultation, representing the Tovata Confederacy before being sent to Lomaiviti.

At home, he is known for creating happy moments, something he said he learnt from his father.

“I’ve always been known as someone who is always happy and like to create happy moments,” he said.

For Ratu Peni, that joy is something worth sharing with others.

item.description: Growing up in Ba was not only a lesson in the value of simplicity because it also laid the foundation for a career in a field which Shweta Shiwangni believes is still largely dominated by men. item.content:encoded:
Growing up in Ba was not only a lesson in the value of simplicity because it also laid the foundation for a career in a field which Shweta Shiwangni believes is still largely dominated by men.

Today, Shweta is a climate officer with the Fiji Meteorological Service, where she has spent the past eight years working in climate monitoring, long-term forecasting and translating complex scientific information into practical advice.

She believes more young women should consider careers in meteorology and not be discouraged by the field’s traditionally male-dominated nature.

“My advice to young girls out there is, if you want to enter this field, feel free to challenge yourselves to pursue this pathway,” she said.

Her journey began in Moto, Ba, where she attended Moto Sanatan Sammelan School before moving to AD Patel College for her secondary education.

Her childhood memories are rooted in the simplicity of village life, a time when access to the internet and other modern conveniences was limited.

She remembers spending time with her parents and cousins, describing simple talanoa sessions and family interactions as among the fondest memories of her upbringing.

Her career path, however, was not always destined for meteorology.

Shweta initially planned to pursue biology, with an interest in marine biology. She later studied environmental science at the University of the South Pacific before beginning her career with the Fiji Meteorological Service.

Her work now includes climate monitoring and long-term predictions for Fiji and other Pacific Island countries, responding to climate data requests and helping translate scientific information into policy recommendations.

She has also worked with regional partners, including the Australian Bureau of Meteorology, on seasonal rainfall forecasts for Fiji’s sugarcane-growing areas.

An important part of her work has been making climate information more accessible.

Through work on gender equality, disability and social inclusion (GEDSI), she has engaged with disability organisations to better understand barriers faced by people accessing meteorological information.

This has included integrating accessibility tools into the Fiji Meteorological Service website, producing seasonal videos and exploring the use of sign language.

Education remains central to creating opportunities.

She encourages young people to study hard, remain focused and continue broadening their qualifications.

“The further you broaden your studies, the more opportunities it will provide for you,” she said.

item.title: PEOPLE I Faithful to the call
item.description: FOR more than four decades, Peni Senikarawa Tamanisau has dedicated his working life to the Seventh-day Adventist Church. A native of Nayavu, Wainibuka, Tailevu, Peni is now responsible for looking after the church-owned sprawling Fulton Tailevu property.
item.content:encoded:
FOR more than four decades, Peni Senikarawa Tamanisau has dedicated his working life to the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

A native of Nayavu, Wainibuka, Tailevu, Peni is now responsible for looking after the church-owned sprawling Fulton Tailevu property.

The once-bustling college campus is now largely vacant. Only four staff quarters are occupied, along with two churches — one serving the Hindi-speaking congregation and the other the iTaukei-speaking worshippers.

Yet for Peni, the stillness of the property does not mean there is little to do.

His responsibilities include maintaining the grounds and buildings, ensuring the property is secure, keeping the surroundings clean and attending to the general upkeep of the site. He is supported by three casual workers who assist him with the demanding work.

Peni approaches his responsibility with the same dedication that has characterised his long association with the Church.

“I like my work because it is executed in a place that is stress-free and full of peace and quiet,” he says.

Peni completed his secondary education at Fulton College in 1989. He later joined the maintenance section of the college, where he worked from 1993 until late 2013, when the institution relocated to its new home in Sabeto, Nadi.

His connection with Fulton Tailevu, however, never really ended.

At the end of 2023, Peni returned to the old campus, this time as its caretaker. Fulton Tailevu was once a vibrant centre of education, drawing students from across the South Pacific. Young people from different island nations came to Fiji to study, live and prepare themselves for service in their communities.

For Peni, caring for such a large and mostly empty property requires more than simply turning up for work.

“You have to like what you do in order to be faithful to the job,” he says.

His commitment is rooted in something deeper than employment.

“Since leaving high school at Fulton College in 1989, I knew I was going to work for the church that educated me and taught me discipline and moral values.”

That sense of calling has sustained him through the years.

“I felt like working for an institution run by the church was my calling, and four decades later I am still here.”

His words reflect a life in which work and faith have become closely intertwined.

“I remained faithful because God has remained faithful to me. I would be earning more if I worked elsewhere, but I currently am satisfied with what I do because I know I would gain more in the long run.”

item.title: PEOPLE | Lessons from the price tag | Former SVC head girl shares real-world money advice
item.description: When Priyanka Mishra returned to Brisbane’s shopping centres after her graduation ceremony, she found herself doing something she had never really done before. Every price tag became a mental calculation.
item.content:encoded:
When Priyanka Mishra returned to Brisbane’s shopping centres after her graduation ceremony, she found herself doing something she had never really done before.

Every price tag became a mental calculation.

Thirty Australian dollars? That was about $F70. Did she really need it?

“Most of the time, I’d quietly put it back on the shelf,” she said.

It was a small habit born out of living on her own savings and one that has shaped her understanding of financial literacy.

Returning to her former school, Swami Vivekananda College, as chief guest at its Financial Literacy Awards, the 2018 head girl shared lessons not drawn out of textbooks, but from personal experience.

She reminded students that everyone’s financial journey is different.

While some receive pocket money, others juggle part-time work or help support their families.

Because circumstances differ, financial success is not measured by income but by the choices people make.

“It’s not about how much money you have, but about the decisions you make with what you have.”

Priyanka also urged students to avoid comparing themselves with others, particularly on social media.

Having stepped away from Instagram two years ago, she said she grew tired of the constant pressure to keep up with carefully curated versions of other people’s lives.

“Comparison is a race nobody ever truly wins, so run your own race and trust your own journey.”

Financial literacy should not mean denying yourself every enjoyment, instead it is about making deliberate choices.

She shared the story of saving for a bungy jump in Queenstown, New Zealand, an experience she had dreamed about for years.

Rather than spending impulsively, she planned and saved until she could afford it.

“I’ll always remember standing on that bridge before taking that leap,” she said, describing it as money well spent on a lifelong memory.

Now working full-time, Priyanka automatically sets aside part of every pay cheque for savings and has begun investing to build for the future.

She does not claim to have mastered personal finance.

“But I realised something – future Priyanka deserves a little help from present Priyanka.”
